comparison: Often released from Pol II host-gene introns; other routes exist
traps: RNA is always unstructured
Single-stranded RNA can form extensive intramolecular helices and tertiary interactions.
All RNAs encode proteins
Functional RNAs such as rRNA and tRNA act as RNA molecules.
Every mRNA has a cap and poly(A) tail
Common eukaryotic architecture has important exceptions, including replication-dependent histone messages.
Transcription +1 equals translation start
They mark separate events; the 5′ UTR can separate them.
Pol II makes only mRNA
Pol II also produces functional noncoding RNAs, including several snRNAs.
Sedimentation coefficients depend on mass, buoyancy and friction, so they are not additive.
5S comes from the mammalian large Pol I precursor
5S is usually a separately synthesized Pol III product.
Cloverleaf is the tertiary shape
It is the secondary-structure representation; the canonical folded tRNA is L-shaped.
The anticodon carries amino acids
The terminal adenosine of the 3′ CCA accepts the amino acid; the anticodon recognizes the codon.
The anticodon alone specifies charging identity
Other identity elements, including acceptor-stem features and discriminator base, can contribute.
All snoRNAs are modification guides
U3 is an important processing-associated snoRNA.
C/D and H/ACA are interchangeable
C/D commonly guides 2′-O-methylation; H/ACA commonly guides pseudouridylation.
A nuclear RNA must function only in the nucleus
Nuclear-encoded rRNAs and tRNAs often function in the cytoplasm.
RNA detection establishes its function
Sequence, assembly, location, modification and direct functional assays provide distinct evidence.
recall: What are the three principal RNA classes directly involved in translation?
mRNA, tRNA and rRNA.
Why can a single RNA strand make a hairpin?
Complementary parts of the strand can pair antiparallel and leave a connecting loop.
What did new RNA association with old ribosomes support?
A replaceable message directing a reusable translation apparatus.
Which rRNAs arise from the typical mammalian Pol I large precursor?
18S, 5.8S and 28S.
Which tRNA end carries an amino acid and which part reads a codon?
3′ terminal A of CCA; the anticodon.
What anticodon written 5′ to 3′ matches 5′-ACG-3′ exactly?
Which snRNAs recognize the early splice site and branch region?
U1 and U2 respectively.
Which snoRNA guide family positions a target ribose for methylation?
Box C/D.
What determines whether an RNP-associated RNA is active?
Proper folding, compatible partners, assembly, localization and any necessary maturation.
Why can protein output fall without a drop in total mRNA?
Translation efficiency, adaptor availability, ribosome function or localization may change.
checklist: Explain the difference between information carried in a coding sequence and information expressed by an RNA fold.
Predict secondary structure and antiparallel pairing; explain compensatory mutations.
Compare common mRNA architectures and state important exceptions.
Identify bacterial and mammalian ribosomal RNAs and explain nonadditive S values.
Describe tRNA cloverleaf, tertiary fold, terminal CCA, anticodon and identity elements.
Distinguish snRNAs and snoRNAs by target, partners, chemical output and location.
Use RNA abundance, precursor processing, fractionation and modification evidence to locate a defect.
Solve steady-state, half-life, coding-length, sedimentation and limiting-component questions.
